articles.title: Served by the court
articles.content: LAST week, the newly established Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) gave two noteworthy judgements. Both concerned legal issues of a political nature — the kind that perhaps would have taken up considerable time and energy in the Supreme Court of the olden days, along with detailed coverage by the media. But those were different times; at present, the cases progressed quietly and the decisions came without much bang or thunder. In one case, the court settled an election dispute that has been going on for the past two years. Back in 2024, the JUI-F had disputed the notification of a woman to one of its reserved seats. It claimed that the woman who had been notified simply shared the first name — Sadaf — with the woman mentioned on the party’s list. The woman on the JUI-F list, Sadaf Yasmin, had decided against submitting her papers due to personal reasons; however, a woman called Sadaf Ihsan (with whom the party says it has no connection) submitted her papers and got nominated by the ECP for the seat. The JUI-F claims Ihsan impersonated Sadaf Yasmin despite having a different name and was somehow identified as the latter. When this waspointed out to the Election Commission of Pakistan, not only did it withdraw the announcement, but also suspended the official who issued the notification. This was reported inDawn. But the matter didn’t end there. Sadaf Ihsan approached the Peshawar High Court (PHC) and was reinstated. The party then challenged the decision in the Supreme Court, winning reprieve for itself. Ihsan was suspended. But the relief was simply an interim order, and once the FCC was established, the file was transferred to it. The FCC sent the case back to the ECP, which in January this yearreinstatedSadaf Ihsan in the seat. This past week, the JUI-F’s appeal against this decision was dismissed by the FCC. Ihsan is now a JUI-F MNA, while the party continues to insist that she is not a member and was never on the list submitted to the ECP. Ihsan, according to a report on the Fafen website, claims she and her family are associated with the party. Three cases, three judgements. But they reveal quite a lot of what the court appears to stand for. It now appears the decision is final and no appellate forums remain. Another interesting aspect of this case is that this seat was given to the JUI-F after the decision that deprived the PTI of reserved seats. In a second case, the FCC has apparentlystopped the PHC from hearingcases regarding the custody or arrest of PTI workers. With the imposition of the emergency in KP and a crackdown against the party in the province, multiple cases concerning the whereabouts or bail of PTI members ended up in the PHC, which then passed an interim order preventing such detentions. As in many cases, bail had also been granted; the provincial government challenged them in the FCC. According to one report inDawn, more than 60 cases in which bail had been given were challenged by the KP government in the FCC. After hearing the cases, the FCC stopped the high court from hearing these matters; its argument was that since the army has been called in, in aid of civil power, the court could no longer hear matters under Article 199, which, in layperson’s terms, is equivalent to what we once saw as the suo motu powers of the Supreme Court. According to one lawyer’s comment, which he posted on social media, this order means the high court can no longer entertain any writ petitions, which, according to him, is a power the courts continued to enjoy even under martial law regimes. In other words, the order limits the PHC in matters far wider than simply the arrests of and bail for PTI workers. It means the high court cannot hear any matters related to fundamental rights. While these two cases date back to just the past week, a third judgement is a little older. It had already been discussed in quite a bit of detail inDawnand elsewhere. But it is still worth mentioning. In a recent case, the FCC seems to have provided arestricted interpretationof workplace harassment. Ignoring past precedents, which had interpreted workplace harassment more liberally, the court has now ruled that harassment is to be limited to actions of an overtly sexual nature; previously, judgements had interpreted the law to include what is defined as gender-based discrimination. Apieceby Barrister Rida Hosain pointed out that in a previous decision, Justice Ayesha Malik had said that “reducing harassment to conduct that is sexual in nature ‘takes away the essence’ of the harassment law, and ignores that harassment is often less about sexual interest and more about reinforcing existing power dynamics”. Hosain quoted Justice Ayesha Malik as saying that the very “purpose of harassment laws is to address gender-based discrimination at the workplace and not to limit it to sexual forms of harassment”. But the FCC has now seen it differently. And while the decision drew criticism, it is fortunate that amendments to the law itself have provided a more wide-ranging definition. However, the ruling of the FCC does mean that complainants in incidents or cases that predate the amendment may have to prove harassment according to the FCC’s interpretation. Women lawyers in particular have discussed this issue in detail in articles and commentary that have appeared inDawn. Three cases, three judgements. But they reveal quite a lot of what the FCC appears to stand for — to those of us who have little understanding of the legalese but who do keep an eye on the politics of the country — be it fundamental rights, women’s rights, or perhaps those of political parties. One can only wonder if any of the parliamentarians who voted for these courts have paid any attention to these judgements.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: A lesson for democracies
articles.content: PROGRESSIVE eyes were riveted on the scintillating victory of Abdul El-Sayed in the US Senate, while celebrating other races that threw up landmark wins for the resurgent left in both Houses of Congress. Just then, a reactionary pushback was making bold strides within the Democratic Party. There’s a word of caution here for far-flung democracies, including South Asia. The lesson seems particularly relevant to India, where a decade-old right-wing government is being challenged on the streets amid hopes for a positive change. El-Sayed’s victory was sweeter as it mocked the Zionist lobby, which had spent an insane amount of money to try and defeat the vehemently pro-Palestine candidate. Worse, El-Sayed’s Democratic rival in the primaries switched sides to back his Republican rival. The joyous news was that James Talarico yanked Texas from its decades-old Republican hold as Annie Andrews took South Carolina, the fiefdom of a rabid Zionist warmonger, the late Lindsey Graham. Adam Hamilton flipped the Republican seat in Kansas, and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota became the first Native American woman to be elected to the Senate. Unsurprisingly, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar retained their seats in the House to the chagrin of Republican xenophobes. Is the left-progressive elation a transient bubble waiting to burst? Those who have witnessed the halcyon days of progressive politics in South Asia — Z.A. Bhutto’s PPP, pre-emergency Indira Gandhi’s Congress, the left radicalism of Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP) in Sri Lanka keeping the welfare state of Sirimavo Bandaranaike on its toes, the socialist populism of Mujibur Rahman, and the idealism infused by Nepal’s communist parties after the collapse of the right-leaning monarchy in their country — would recognise the reactionary pushback being witnessed within the Democratic Party in the US all too well. It so happens that Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries are both deeply linked with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). Schumer is positioning himself as the Senate majority leader while Jeffries fancies his chances as Speaker of the House of Representatives. Democrat socialists who helped flip the House and Senate from the Republicans are strongly opposing both men but with faint hopes of success. The idea was essentially honed in the UK. We can have a Tony Blair-led Labour with the leftists in the party critiquing him with incremental effect, if at all. Is the left-progressive elation a transient bubble waiting to burst? As AIPAC allies, neither Schumer nor Jeffries had opposed Joe Biden’s arms supplies to Israel during the war in Gaza. It’s a forceful critique of this duplicitous Democratic policy that has contributed substantially to the socialist bloc leading the amazing victory in both Houses of Congress. Both institutional leaders, Schumer and Jeffries, repeatedly took active steps to protect and sustain the flow of US weapons shipments, even as the Democratic Party’s progressive wing pushed to cut them off. During multiple critical legislative pushes, Schumer consistently voted against amendments brought by progressive senators attempting to block or condition offensive weapons transfers to Israel. Both leaders separate their disdain for Benjamin Netanyahu from their institutional commitment to the Israeli military. They maintain that the US-Israel defence relationship must remain robust, ensuring that the supply of weapons continues regardless of internal party pressure over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. Their politics may not be too different in this regard from Israel’s opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s, whose contempt for Netanyahu is as legendary as his zeal to destroy the lives of Palestinians in Gaza. The quandary is widespread. Rahul Gandhi, for example, can be likened to the progressive socialist bloc in the Democratic Party. Like the US Democrats and UK Labour, his party leadership remained heavily dependent on corporate funding. Its senior leaders and elite technocrats have resisted moving back to a left-populist stance. For years, Congress watchers say, the party was effectively trapped in a ‘no-man’s-land’ — too market-friendly to appeal to the radical left, too secular to win back religious nationalists, and too stained by legacy corruption scandals to win over the aspirational youth. Recognising that chasing the corporate-centrist consensus resulted in near-extinction, Rahul Gandhi is attempting a significant left-populist pivot to break the unpopularity loop. Through massive nationwide foot marches like the Unite India March, he seeks to recast Congress as a grassroots movement against crony capitalism, corporate monopolies, and right-wing social polarisation. The Gandhi messaging has explicitly pivoted towards aggressive anti-corporate rhetoric, demanding a national caste census, advocating for wealth redistribution, and focusing heavily on rural distress and massive youth unemployment. By directly challenging the corporate and religious alliances that define the ruling establishment, Rahul is trying to shed the legacy of 1991. Yet, internal friction between generational leaders means that climbing out of their unpopular mode remains an uphill structural battle. Would Rahul be able to buck the trend observed in India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka most prominently? Benazir Bhutto’s politics mirrored that of Western centre-left leaders of her era, such as Tony Blair and Bill Clinton. She repositioned the PPP into a ‘Third Way’ social democratic party. Instead of the state owning the means of production to guarantee ‘roti, kapra aur makaan’, she believed a free-market economy should generate wealth, while the state’s role was merely to provide a social safety net for the poorest. Thus, Benazir is said to have reassured the Pakistani elite, Washington, and international financial institutions that a return of the PPP did not mean a return to her father’s economics. As with the JVP, which finds itself kowtowing to the IMF despite years of hostility to it, Rahul Gandhi’s regional satraps remain in cahoots with the very business tycoons he calls out as toxic. There’s a redeeming feature here, though. Rahul shares with the leftist Democrats who roundly defeated Donald Trump their sharp critique of Zionism. Sadly, the Marxist-Leninist JVP hides behind diplomatic verbiage. It could learn from another JVP — Jewish Voice for Peace — that calls out Israel’s actions in Gaza as gruesome genocide. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Economic ills
articles.content: DESPITE an oversold stabilisation, many of our economy’s vital signs continue to falter. The economy resembles a patient out of the ICU but still in hospital. Since 2024, our per capita GDP growth has been near zero — sadly, South Asia’s slowest recorded pace. Even our recent growth spurts, brief and import-led, have given way to longer busts, draining reserves and sending us back to the IMF’s tough terms that extend low growth. Once near the region’s top performers in per capita GDP, we now risk falling to the bottom. As incomes stall, poverty rises. Our extreme poverty rate (23 per cent) isnear the bottom regionally. It’s about 10 times India’s, against near parity in 2011. Our GDP’s composition tells a bleak tale too. It’s consumption-heavy (82pc) but investment-light (14pc) — on both counts among the region’s worst. India and China invest over 30pc of GDP, creating jobs and capacity for today and later — much better than our consumption binges. Limiting job, technology, and export growth, industry’s share has been nearly a fifth for over 50 years versus a quarter in India and Sri Lanka and a third in Bangladesh. Low investment causes low growth, but its origins and destinations matter too. We court foreign capital while ignoring local capital. Foreign capital must earn and save more dollars than it repatriates and create jobs and local capacity. But we get it mostly in domestic sectors, which later depletes reserves. Unlike our peers, we chase a few rich states for capital rather than prioritising diversified private capital. We shun creative ways to boost local savings and capital. So, we remain capital-starved — yet we quickly drain reserves and risk the haughty whims of rich states. Capital droughts in export sectors cause dollar and job droughts. From a peak of 17pc in 1992, exports now barely reach a tenth of our GDP — South Asia’s second-lowest share, below even Afghanistan’s. Low-quality compounds low quantity. Harvard’s Economic Complexity Index ranks us 89th among 145 states. So our exports face intense competition but return little. Exports rarely cover imports, creating large trade gaps. Remittances partly plug the gap. But exports keep workers at home and families intact, create jobs, earn dollars, and pay taxes. Remittances separate families and often don’t create jobs or pay taxes directly. They frequently fuel consumption, while exports are fuelled by investment. Remittances now almost equal our exports, as it is easier to send workers abroad than goods (India earns six times as much from exports as from remittances). Even so, we often run large external deficits that lead to a crisis as booms turn into busts. Low growth and weak efforts leave our coffers lean. Tax revenues barely reach 11pc of GDP — which is among South Asia’s lowest. Indirect anti-poor taxes provide about half our tax target, down from about two-thirds in 2021-22. New direct taxes further burden the wallets of salaried persons and formal industry, while favoured sectors pay low taxes. Spending prioritises upkeep over uplift. Expenditure hogs over 90 paisas out of every federal budget rupee; development consoles itself with just five. These twin deficits force us to keep our borrowing bowl out. Our public debt-to-GDP ratio of 73pc is lower than the Japanese and Singaporean levels of over 150pc. But our repayment muscle better depicts our debt overhang. On the share of federal outlays spent on interest alone, we rank among the worst globally. We use debt not only to invest or meet recurrent expenses but also to beef up reserves. IMF debt and deposits by rich states, which impose odious economic and political conditions on us, now exceed even our highest-ever reserves. These dreary metrics mirror a sinking economy. Low investment and import-led growth widen the twin deficits to swell debt. Interest outlays then leave little money for growth, creating a vicious circle. A weak economy reflects perverse politics. Poor countries need both a developmental and a welfare state. Ours is a parasitic and apathetic state run by rapacious rulers. This isn’t a tragedy of ineptitude alone: willing rulers can easily hire merit. It’s a deliberate design by kleptocrats who may lose their wealth and power if there is real progress. Nor is this the tale of a few eras. Our autocracies, too, delivered short-term growth, leading to conflict and undercutting future progress. Ideas abound on how to pursue sound progress, but minds that will champion and implement them well do not. Only democracy and civilian sway will bring such minds to the helm of affairs. The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 30 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.
articles.author: Dr Niaz Murtaza

articles.title: Missing discussion
articles.content: IN contrast to official claims of economic stability, a series of recently released reports provide disturbing evidence of deepening poverty and a human development crisis in Pakistan. According to the World Bank’s Pakistan Poverty and Equitybrief, the national poverty rate spiralled from 22 per cent in 2018-19 to 29pc in 2024-25 — meaning that about 70 million poor people across the country live below the national poverty line. The Gini index, a measure of economic inequality, has increased from 28.4pc to 32.7pc, the highest in 25 years. The World Bank’s regional economic outlook reported that Pakistan is home to about half of the MENAAP region’s population that falls under the extremely poor category. The World Bank attributes Pakistan’s reversal in poverty reduction to economic shocks triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic, the devastating 2022 floods, high inflation, and currency depreciation. The UNDP’s 2025 Global Multidimensional Poverty Indexreportedthat 38.3pc of Pakistan’s population (95m people) is multidimensionally poor — deprived not just of cash but also of necessities such as healthcare and education. Another 32m people are vulnerable to multidimensional poverty. Pakistan’s poor population of 38.3pc dwarfed India’s 16.4pc and Bangladesh’s 14.9pc. The alarming scale of deprivation was also reflected in the 2026 Global Hunger Index, whichplacedPakistan 106th among 122 countries. Pakistan has the highest hunger score in South Asia. The report attributes food price inflation to declining household purchasing power and constrained access to food. It finds that undernourishment in the country climbed from ‘low’ in 2018 to ‘medium’, while child wasting has risen towards the ‘high’ threshold. Poverty is rooted in decades of misguided public policy. All these reports reflect the severity of the crisis. A nationally representative mental health survey (2018-22), published in the British Medical Journal, revealed distressing facts. Thesurveyfound that every third Pakistani lives with a diagnosable mental or behavioural disorder; one in five meets the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder. A shocking 6pc reported suicidal thoughts, and more than one in 10 had depression. Such staggering rates of mental disorders have been linked to lower income and poor education, unemployment, age, and disrupted family circumstances. Human development has remained a chronically ignored priority in Pakistan. The UNDP’s Human Development Report 2025 placed Pakistan 168th out of 193 countries appearing in the ‘low’ human development category. Except for Afghanistan, all regional countries ranked ahead of Pakistan on the Human Development Index. Poverty is rooted in decades of misguided public policy and bad governance. Human development has been given cosmetic importance — the subject is mostly confined to official speeches and election manifestos. Although Covid-19, the floods, and broader climate change have battered the economy, human development seldom features on the government’s list of priorities. Geopolitical and ongoing border tensions, and more recently theGulf warshocks, have diverted resources and attention from human development to security priorities. The issue has been further compounded by internal security challenges that have held back exports and stifled foreign investment. Terrorism in two provinces and the poor law and order situation have shattered local investments. This environment has forced many foreign companies to pack up and withdraw capital from our markets. Agriculture — for long the bedrock of the national economy and a source of food security for millions — has been systematically eroded in recent decades. Sharp increases in agri-input prices, a poorly managed water sector, rapid land degradation, and exploitative market forces have wrecked this critical sector. Soaring energy prices, an unreliable grid, and a huge tax burden, including petroleum surcharges, have made energy exorbitant for the farm sector. Crippling increases in petroleum prices have pushed up transport fares, raising the cost of the farm-to-market supply chain. The resulting food inflation has forced millions of families to compromise on their diet. Sadly, even though poverty and hunger have emerged as an existential challenge for millions of families in Pakistan, a national focus on these issues is absent. These issues rarely find space in the national discourse — especially on electronic media, which remains abuzz with hysterical talk shows on subjects like governor’s rule and new provinces. Distracting the masses from the real issues and failing to include critical report findings will not reduce the citizens’ frustration. The writer is senior adviser, water governance, at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute.
articles.author: Naseer Memon

articles.title: Restructuring plans
articles.content: NO matter how strongly the PPP, a key coalition partner,wishes to see it buried, the push for new administrative units and provinces seems to be picking up steam once again. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif brought the issue into the limelight on Sunday,telling an interviewerthat the country could have as many as 12 new provinces if the exercise were driven by administrative needs rather than ethnic, linguistic, or political considerations. Yet in Pakistan, redrawn boundaries always carry ethnic and political weight. Speculation about a possible administrative restructuring has intensified of late, with talk of it soon being accomplished through a 28th amendment to the Constitution. It is also suggested that while the amendment may be fast-tracked, perhaps wrapped up within the year, its actual implementation will be deferred until after the next general election because of the formidable legal and administrative challenges involved in redistributing the state’s resources equitably. But if the implementation can wait, why not the legislation? The government may be tempted to push ahead while it can still count on a majority in parliament, but a majority alone is not a consensus. A proposal of such immense national import demands nothing less. The Election Commission’s botched conduct of the 2024 general election has also left serious, lingering doubts about how far the current legislature represents the public will — doubts that might taint any constitutional change of this magnitude that it passes. It would, therefore, be a much wiser move, politically speaking, to take up any debate on administrative restructuring again after the next general election. In the interim, parliament should pursue electoral reforms with the opposition to ensure that the commission does not repeat its 2024 mistakes, so that the next election earns the public’s trust and yields a legislature whose mandate is beyond doubt. Until then, the federal and provincial governments should at least make an effort to revive the local government structure and give it a fair chance to prove its efficacy as a means of public service delivery. Most arguments in favour of new administrative units circle back to a few central ideas, chief among which is the failure of provincial governments to ensure that resources allocated to them reach the people. The LG system was designed to be that last-mile tier of governance that would make this possible, but, sadly, successive civilian governments have failed to operationalise it effectively, preferring instead to concentrate administrative, political and financial power in a few provincial centres. Population growth and internal migration have sharply increased pressures on existing administrative centres in recent decades, but empowered LGs can redistribute that burden without redrawing provincial boundaries. It is up to the political leadership to choose between these two paths.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Extreme heat
articles.content: CLIMATE change is already taking itstollon Pakistan’s farm sector. Crop yields are falling, livestock productivity is declining, fertile land is becoming uncultivable, and food insecurity is rising. Alongside, rural incomes are shrinking, and both cash and food poverty are increasing. It is against this backdrop that a new UN assessment — Extreme Heat and Agriculture — by the Food and Agriculture Organisation and the World Meteorological Organisation has sought to underscore the rapid erosion of farm productivity, especially in rain-fed regions, and its impact on rural households owing to rising temperatures across the country. The findings are particularly worrying for Punjab, where frequent and severeheatwavesare disrupting rural livelihoods. Fruit productivity in the province’s high-rainfall areas has halved. Livestock is suffering, with heat stress reducing milk production and increasing the incidence of diseases among small ruminants. The consequences are not confined to farms. Lower output means reduced incomes for farming households, with extreme temperatures accelerating the spoilage of vegetables, dairy products, and other perishables. Families earn and eat less. Gender inequality deepens the problem. Ruralwomen, who undertake considerable agricultural and household work, face prolonged exposure to extreme temperatures. Pregnant and lactating women are particularly vulnerable, with a sharp increase in the risk of premature births during severe heatwaves. However, climate adaptation is yet to find a place in our agricultural policies. The effects of rising temperatures on the sector that sustains two-thirds of the population cannot be mitigated with input subsidies, crop support prices, or procurement targets. Farmers need heat-resistant crop varieties, better water managementtechnology, and access to modern farming machinery.Investmentin cold storage, efficient supply chains and public and livestock health services is equally important. Agricultural research requires greater private investment and better human resources. Without tweaking policies to respond to the climate challenge, repeated heatwaves will erode productivity, making farming less viable for smallholders. The problem crosses the border. Both sides of Punjab face the same climate challenges, requiring Pakistan and India to cooperate on farm resilience. Heat is already cutting into rural incomes and into what families can afford to eat. Farm policies that ignore it will fail the people they are meant to support.
articles.author: Editorial
